title: EDHEC Private Equity, VC & M&A — Final Exam 2024
notice: Derived study pack: questions are condensed and paraphrased from the 2024 EDHEC past paper; numerical answers and worked solutions are reproduced. The scanned source 7017_69368.pdf was visually reviewed page by page: its seven printed exam pages match this 2024 pack, while the seven reverse sides are blank; the scan is therefore tracked as a duplicate source and is not counted as a fourth exam. IMPORTANT: the official file contains no marked MCQ answers, so the MCQ answer key in this pack is derived (inferred), not official — treat MCQ grading as practice only; the worked/numerical solutions are reproduced from the official file.

questions.prompt: What does 'first closing' mean in private-equity fundraising?

choices.text: The point at which the fund starts investing.
The stage when the fund reaches its minimum required commitments to begin operations.
The deadline for all LPs to make initial capital contributions.
The stage when the manager finalizes total commitments.

questions.solution: First closing is when the fund has enough committed capital (the minimum size) to start investing; later closings add LPs.

questions.prompt: A 'catch-up' clause in private equity typically refers to:

choices.text: Allocating the first profits to LPs to meet the hurdle rate.
Adjusting portfolio valuation to market conditions.
Allocating profits disproportionately to GPs after LPs reach the hurdle rate.
Reinvesting distributions into follow-on investments.

questions.solution: After the LP hurdle, the catch-up gives the GP a disproportionate share of subsequent profits until the 80/20 split is restored.

questions.prompt: Which best explains the J-curve in private equity?

choices.text: Performance dips early due to fees and initial losses, then rises as value is created.
Portfolio companies grow exponentially through operational improvements.
Initial distributions are delayed until all investments exit.
GP compensation rises exponentially as the fund matures.

questions.solution: Early management fees and write-downs push returns below zero; later exits and value creation lift them.

questions.prompt: EBITDA is a proxy for:

choices.text: Sales.
Operating cash flow.
Growth.
Debt.

questions.solution: EBITDA approximates operating cash flow before capex, working capital, interest and taxes.

questions.prompt: Which characteristic represents an attractive growth-equity candidate?

choices.text: Early-stage company with no product-market fit.
Mature company with stagnant growth and limited scalability.
Significant revenue growth, proven product-market fit and scaling potential.
Company requiring heavy restructuring and capex.

questions.solution: Growth equity funds proven models into scaling, not turnarounds or unproven startups.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an anti-dilution clause?

choices.text: To prevent existing investor ownership from being diluted in future rounds.
To restrict new shares issued to employees.
To limit founders' ability to issue equity.
To ensure debt is paid before equity.

questions.solution: It adjusts the preferred conversion price in a down round.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between seed-stage and Series A?

choices.text: Series A investors typically require board seats.
Seed focuses on scaling; Series A on product-market fit.
Seed builds and validates the product; Series A scales the business.
Series A requires higher founder equity stakes.

questions.solution: Seed validates; Series A scales a repeatable model.

questions.prompt: In venture capital, pre-money valuation is:

choices.text: Always higher than post-money.
Always lower than post-money.
Lower than post-money if the venture progresses after investment.
Lower than post-money if the entrepreneur negotiates well.

questions.solution: Post-money = pre-money + investment.

questions.prompt: The key inputs of the VC valuation model are:

choices.text: Investment, time-to-exit, exit value, hurdle rate.
Investment, time-to-exit, exit value, risk-free rate, risk premium.
Investment, number of rounds, exit value, hurdle rate.
Investment, number of rounds, exit value, risk-free rate, risk premium.

questions.solution: The standard VC method uses I, t, exit value and hurdle.

questions.prompt: Palooka Products receives $5m today, exits at $50m in 5 years, VC hurdle 40%. What equity share does the VC require?
Which financing structure most likely improves equity IRR in an LBO?

choices.text: Increasing subordinated debt.
Reducing the equity contribution and increasing leverage.
Interest-only senior debt in early years.
Replacing floating-rate debt with fixed-rate debt.

questions.solution: More leverage means less equity for the same enterprise, so the equity return is magnified (if the deal performs).

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a dividend recapitalization?

choices.text: Return capital to investors while retaining ownership.
Reduce the company's debt burden.
Raise new equity for growth.
Refinance debt at a lower rate.

questions.solution: The portfolio company borrows to pay a dividend to the sponsor, returning cash without an exit.

questions.prompt: Which represents an attractive LBO candidate?

choices.text: Stable margins, low capex, declining industry.
Strong cash flow, low leverage, cyclical demand.
High margins, strong free cash flow, dominant position in a fragmented but stable industry.
High growth, high retention, high working-capital needs and R&D.

questions.solution: Stable, cash-generative, defensible businesses support debt service.

questions.prompt: An LBO target is bought for $1,500m with $500m equity. After 5 years no debt is repaid and EV rises by $500m. What is the cash-on-cash multiple?
questions.solution: Entry debt = 1,000; exit EV = 2,000; exit equity = 1,000; 1,000/500 = 2x.

questions.prompt: CFO $125m, CFI $50m, mandatory debt repayment $30m, cash from balance sheet $20m. Cash available for optional debt repayment?
What is most critical when identifying buyers in a sell-side M&A transaction?

choices.text: Ability to secure financing.
Alignment with the seller's strategic objectives and valuation expectations.
Experience in previous M&A deals.
Ability to retain management.

questions.solution: Strategic fit and price expectations determine whether a buyer is credible and likely to close.

questions.prompt: Which metric is most commonly used in merger-consequences analysis?

choices.text: EV/EBITDA.
Return on equity.
Earnings per share.
Internal rate of return.

questions.solution: Merger consequences focus on EPS accretion/dilution for the acquirer.

questions.prompt: Discuss how financial-market conditions may affect the valuation of a new venture.
questions.answer: In the VC method, value depends on exit value, hurdle rate and time to exit. Interest rates raise hurdle rates and lower multiples; risk appetite lowers hurdles and raises multiples; liquidity affects both entry and exit; inflation affects projected revenue/EBITDA and multiples.
questions.solution: Structure: the three inputs; then rates, sentiment, liquidity and inflation, each with direction of effect.

questions.prompt: Do you agree that 'investor liquidation rights are fundamentally a way to force founders to do investors' will and should be resisted'?
questions.answer: No. Liquidation rights protect the investor's downside and enforce the need for an exit, which is necessary to return capital to LPs. They are tough but within fair practice; the real issue is calibration (preference size, participation, caps), not the existence of the right.
questions.solution: Take a clear position, explain the economic function (downside protection, exit discipline, LP liquidity) and qualify with the cost to founders.

questions.prompt: Discuss the trade-offs created by staged financing for the entrepreneur.
questions.answer: Advantages: progressively higher valuations, less dilution, strategic discipline. Disadvantages: funding risk if milestones are missed, short-termism, less freedom to pivot, dependence on market conditions at each round.
questions.solution: Give both sides and a conclusion: staging is efficient but shifts risk to the founder.

questions.prompt: What are four key credit statistics used to size LBO debt?
questions.answer: Total debt/EBITDA; senior debt/EBITDA; EBITDA interest coverage; fixed-charge coverage; debt-service coverage.
questions.solution: Any four of the five are accepted; explain that they cap leverage and protect lenders.

questions.prompt: Why have strategic buyers traditionally been able to outbid financial buyers in auctions?
questions.answer: Synergies (cost and revenue), a longer investment horizon, and cheaper/less constrained financing. Financial buyers need a 3-7 year exit and are limited by debt coverage.
questions.solution: Explain synergy value, horizon and cost of capital; note that financial buyers can still win when synergies are low or financing is cheap.

questions.prompt: Magical Genie: VW offers $2m at a $5m post-money; XY offers $1m at a $3m pre-money. Founder owns 3m shares. Sale at $10m after one year. Scenario 1 (75%): $1m more at $2/share. Scenario 2 (25%): $2m more at $0.25/share.

parts.prompt: Initial round: compute pre/post-money, price, investor shares, total shares and founder ownership.
parts.answer: VW: pre $3m, post $5m, price $1, 2m shares, 5m total, founder 60%. XY: pre $3m, post $4m, price $1, 1m shares, 4m total, founder 75%.

parts.prompt: Second round under both scenarios: new shares and founder ownership.
parts.answer: Scenario 1: VW 60%; XY 0.5m new, 4.5m total, founder 66.7%. Scenario 2: VW 4m new, 9m total, founder 33.3%; XY 8m new, 12m total, founder 25%.
parts.solution: Shares issued = amount / price. Scenario 1: 1/2=0.5m. Scenario 2: 1/0.25=4m and 2/0.25=8m.

parts.prompt: Compute expected founder wealth with 75% probability on Scenario 1 and recommend an offer.
If the angels used a complex VC term sheet instead of common equity, which part of the calculations would change?
parts.answer: The exit-value distribution, not the ownership maths: liquidation preferences, participation and anti-dilution change the split between founder and investor, so the founder's expected wealth falls.
parts.solution: Preferred terms reallocate exit proceeds; ownership fractions can stay the same while payoffs change.

questions.prompt: Alma PE buys Apfel at 8x LTM EBITDA and exits after 2 years at 8.5x. 60% term-loan debt at 10% with cash sweep; management rolls over 10% of equity, sponsor funds 90%. LTM revenue $100m, +10% p.a.; EBITDA margin 35%, then 38%, then 40%. NWC and capex 10% of revenue; depreciation 10% of revenue; 0% tax.

parts.prompt: Compute revenue, EBITDA, entry EV and exit EV ($m).
parts.answer: Revenue 100 / 110 / 121; EBITDA 35 / 41.8 / 48.4; entry EV $280m; exit EV $411.4m.
parts.solution: Revenue grows 10%. EBITDA = margin × revenue. EV = 8×35 = 280 entry; 8.5×48.4 = 411.4 exit.

parts.prompt: Compute CFADS, interest, FCF and debt for each year ($m).
parts.solution: The official solution table uses NWC = 10% of EBITDA, although the case wording says 10% of revenue: 10%×35 = 3.50; 10%×41.8 = 4.18 → ΔNWC = 0.68; 10%×48.4 = 4.84 → ΔNWC = 0.66. Capex is 10% of revenue: 11.00 and 12.10. CFADS = EBITDA - ΔNWC - capex. Interest = 10% of opening debt (16.80 then 15.47). FCF = CFADS - interest; debt falls by FCF.

parts.prompt: Compute entry/exit equity, sponsor equity cheque, return, CCM and IRR. Invest?
parts.answer: Entry equity $112m; sponsor cheque $100.8m; exit equity $276.89m; proceeds $249.20m; return $148.40m; CCM 2.47x; IRR 57.2%; yes.
parts.solution: Equity = EV - debt. Sponsor funds 90% of 112 = 100.8. Exit equity = 411.4 - 134.51 = 276.89. Management rolls over 10%, so the sponsor owns 90% of the exit equity: 90% × 276.89 = 249.20. Return = 249.20 - 100.80 = 148.40. CCM = 249.20/100.80 = 2.47x; IRR = 2.47^(1/2) - 1 = 57.2%. Yes, the deal clears the LBO hurdle.

parts.prompt: Decompose the return into EBITDA, multiple and net-debt effects.
parts.answer: Official solution: EBITDA impact $96.48m (65.0%), multiple impact $21.78m (14.7%), net-debt impact $30.14m (20.3%).
parts.solution: Use the case's decomposition: EBITDA impact = ΔEBITDA × entry multiple; multiple impact = Δmultiple × exit EBITDA; net-debt impact = entry debt - exit debt. The three sum to the $148.40m return.
